analysis.one_liner: Bans children's products containing any lead, treating them as banned hazardous substances.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee; the Senate never held a vote on banning lead in children's products.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would declare any product marketed to or foreseeably used by children under age 7 that contains lead to be a banned hazardous substance under federal law. It set lead limits of 0.02% by weight for children's jewelry and 0.04% for other children's products, applying even when the lead is not accessible to a child. It also directed the Consumer Product Safety Commission to consider even stricter limits. The bill was introduced in September 2007, during a wave of recalls of lead-tainted children's products.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and young children, who would be protected from lead exposure through toys, jewelry, and other products marketed to kids under 7. The bill's findings cite well-documented links between lead and neurological damage, developmental delays, and learning problems, and note the Consumer Product Safety Commission had recalled more than 50 lead-containing children's products since 1998.

how_it_helps.text: Any children's product containing lead above the set thresholds would be treated as a banned hazardous substance, prohibiting its sale in interstate commerce regardless of whether the lead is accessible to a child.

The bill sets lead limits of 0.02% by weight for children's jewelry and 0.04% for other children's products, and directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission to consider lower thresholds within two years.

The bill's findings document that lead exposure in children can cause neurological damage, delayed development, learning deficiencies, hearing problems, and in rare cases death, and that lead accumulates in the body so even small exposures add to the risk.

analysis.who_pays: Toy makers, children's jewelry manufacturers, and importers, who would have to eliminate lead from their products or keep those products off the U.S. market, bearing testing, reformulation, and compliance costs.

drawbacks.text: The ban applies without regard to whether the lead is accessible to children, so products with trace amounts of lead sealed inside components — and not reachable by a child — would still be barred, which critics would call overbroad for cases where exposure risk is negligible.

Manufacturers and importers of children's products would bear compliance costs, including testing and reformulation to meet the 0.02% (jewelry) and 0.04% (other products) thresholds, costs that could fall hardest on smaller importers and sellers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: the bill's own findings document permanent neurological harm from even small lead exposures in children, and the cost side is ordinary manufacturing compliance that many products would have met anyway. The main design question is the zero-tolerance approach that ignores lead accessibility, which sweeps in some negligible-risk products. On balance, the benefit to children's health outweighs the compliance cost, but the bill was written broadly and a careful committee process would likely have adjusted the accessibility question.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on September 11, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was ever taken: the bill stayed in the Commerce Committee and never came to the Senate floor before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
The bill attracted two Democratic cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Toy and children's jewelry manufacturers and importers who faced stricter lead rules in this bill were spared them when it died in committee; the bill's Senate sponsors had no mechanism to force the committee to act.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban lead-containing children's products and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no opposition is recorded; the bill's three sponsors were all Democrats, and the committee that held it was chaired by a Democrat.

industries.industry: Toy and children's product manufacturers and importers
industries.note: The bill would have barred any children's product containing lead above 0.04% by weight from interstate commerce, forcing testing and reformulation costs. It died in committee, so no costs were imposed.
Children's jewelry would have faced the strictest limit in the bill, 0.02% lead by weight of any part. The industry continued selling under the looser rules in place at the time.
